newsitem.title: USA: Arkansas pair settles SEC insider trading charges.
newsitem.headline: Arkansas pair settles SEC insider trading charges.

text.p: An Arkansas man and his father-in-law agreed to pay nearly $222,000 to settle insider trading charges, the Securities and Exchange Commission said Tuesday.

The two Little Rock residents, David Schmidt, 38, and his father-in-law Willard Whitehurst, 59, neither admitted nor denied allegations by the SEC, filed in a civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

In its complaint filed Tuesday, the SEC alleged that in September 1994 Whitehurst learned of negotiations between Mark IV Industries and Purolator Products Co. during his employment with Dayco Products Inc., a subsidiary of Mark IV.

The complaint alleged that Whitehurst asked Schmidt to buy $10,000 worth of Puralotor's common stock and then tipped him of the negotiations. Schmidt also recommended Purolator stock to three other persons.
Collectively, Whitehurst, Schmidt and Schmidt's colleagues bought 15,173 Purolator common shares. Following the public announcement, the group sold or tendered their shares for a profit of $109,483.
Schmidt agreed to pay $105,242 in alleged insider-trading derived profits, interest of $23,333 and a civil penalty of $68,207.
Whitehurst agreed to turn over $4,241 in alleged ill-gotten gains, interest of $940 and a civil penalty of $19,827, the agency said.
Purolator, based in Tulsa, Okla., was a maker of filtration products and systems. Mark IV, based in Amherst, N.Y., makes power and fluid transfer products, transportation and audio products.
Dayco Products is based in Miamisburg, Ohio.
